doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Al Hibbler, Monty Alexander and being refused service in Miami
summary: With Hibbler in Miami in 1965, he met Monty Alexander and a waitress refused to serve 'the colored'.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: good experience. But then when that ran dry I went to work with Al Hibbler. And Al Hibbler and I were in Miami, Florida, playing in a hotel/bar type place that had a restaurant. This was in 1965. And as a matter of fact this was the same year I met Monty Alexander. Monty came in that same night and played with us. I told him I said, “Look, this is my number, you come up to New York I’ll get you some work. You play too good to be down here, man, come up to New York.” He was 18 years old I think and he came up. Anyway after we got through with the gig Al wanted to get something to eat. Well we were in the bar and the restaurant was right next door. You’d go out of the bar and you’d go right into the restaurant. And we were staying in the same motel. We get into the restaurant, I’d lead Al in through the door, and instead of walking all the way in we sat right there by the door. The stools were kind of high for me. They weren’t too high for Al. So I kind of ambled my way up there and we’re sitting there for a while and nobody shows up. Finally I said, “Waitress, waitress.” And she came over and she says, “We don’t serve the colored.” Just like that. It caught me off guard completely because we’d been playing all night long. And no sooner that she said we don’t serve the colored here comes two great big cops in the door, they walked right in. They says, “You having trouble here, Annie?” And Al says, “Let’s go.” You know we got up and went right back into the bar where we were. It was a kind of a close call because I was a hothead in those days, I was a young nut. I mean like I said, these two great big guys were as tall as the lamps. They could have swiped me out with one blow. But I had kind of a hot temper in those days, you know how we are.
